title: Component inputs and outputs
goal: Pass data into child components and send events back up to parents.

concepts: input() and input.required() for data coming in (they're signals)
output() and .emit() for events going out
Binding in the parent: [course]="c" and (saved)="onSaved($event)"
model() for two-way binding [(value)]
Smart (container) vs presentational (dumb) components
Data flows down, events flow up

resources.title: Angular: Accepting data with input properties

build.task: In angular-playground, split course-list into: course-card (presentational: input.required<Course>(), outputs saveToggled and enrolled), course-filters (presentational: model() for query and level so the parent can use [(query)] and [(level)]), and course-page (smart: owns the signals and logic). Add a quantity-stepper component with model<number>() plus min/max inputs, and use it inside course-card for 'seats'. course-card must not import any service or change any state itself.
acceptance: course-card uses input.required and emits outputs; it has no state of its own except UI-only state
course-filters uses model() and the parent binds with [( )]
course-page owns all state signals and handles events
quantity-stepper respects min and max inputs
Everything still works: filter, save toggle, counts

hints: Child: course = input.required<Course>(); saveToggled = output<number>(); In the template: (click)="saveToggled.emit(course().id)".
Parent template: <app-course-card [course]="c" (saveToggled)="toggle($event)" />. $event is the emitted value.
model: query = model(''); in the child's input: (input)="query.set(...)". Parent: <app-course-filters [(query)]="query" /> where query is the parent's signal.

explainBack.q: Trace what happens from clicking 'Save' on a card to the saved count updating.
lookFor: new input flows down to card

explainBack.q: Why shouldn't course-card change state itself?
lookFor: single source of truth in the parent

lastHintExplanation: Data flows down through inputs and events flow up through outputs. The card emits 'saveToggled' with the id; the parent's handler updates its signal; computed values recalculate; and the new course object flows back down into the card's input. Keeping state in one smart parent makes cards reusable and predictable.

predict.q: Child: name = input('Guest'). Parent uses <app-greet /> with no binding. What is name() in the child?
predict.why: The default value is used when the parent doesn't bind the input.

title: Services and dependency injection
goal: Move shared state and logic into services and inject them where needed.

concepts: What a service is: a class for logic/state that isn't UI
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) gives one shared instance
inject(ServiceName) inside components and other services
Signal-based state in a service: private writable signal, public readonly
Why DI: testability and swapping implementations
Component-level providers (a new instance per component) — just know it exists

build.task: Create CourseStore (ng g s course-store): it owns courses, query and level signals (private writable, exposed as readonly with asReadonly()), computed filtered and savedCount, and methods toggleSaved, enroll, setQuery and setLevel. It also persists saved ids with an effect. Refactor course-page to inject the store instead of owning state. Create a header-badge component that injects the same store and shows 'Saved: N' in the app header, proving both components share one instance. Write a short docs/di.md explaining DI with your own example.
acceptance: State lives in CourseStore; components have no duplicated state
Writable signals are private; components only read via readonly signals and call methods
header-badge and course-page show consistent numbers (same instance)
Persistence still works
docs/di.md explains DI with your own example

hints: private readonly _courses = signal<Course[]>(...); readonly courses = this._courses.asReadonly();
In a component: private store = inject(CourseStore); then use store.filtered() in the template (make store protected or public so the template can see it).
providedIn: 'root' means Angular creates one instance the first time something injects it, and everyone gets that same one.
proof: Commit with the store and refactored components.

explainBack.q: Why expose readonly signals and methods instead of the writable signals?
lookFor: only the store can change state
all changes go through named methods

explainBack.q: How do header-badge and course-page end up with the same data?

lastHintExplanation: providedIn: 'root' registers one app-wide instance, so every inject(CourseStore) gets the same object, and both components read the same signals. Keeping writable signals private and exposing readonly ones plus methods means state only changes through named actions, which makes bugs easy to trace.

options: No, each gets its own copy

title: Building a task board with a signal store
goal: Build a small Kanban-style task board with a service store and several cooperating components.

concepts: Designing state for a feature: tasks with status columns
Derived state per column with computed
Moving items between lists immutably
Component tree: board → column → task-card, plus a new-task form
Persisting store state

build.task: In angular-playground, add a /board page (just render it in app for now; routing comes next week). TaskStore holds tasks: { id, title, status: 'todo' | 'doing' | 'done', priority: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high', createdAt }. Components: board (3 columns), column (input: status, title), task-card (shows priority colour, buttons ← → to move, delete), and new-task-form (title + priority). Show counts per column, sort each column by priority, and persist to localStorage. Bonus: drag and drop with the Angular CDK.
acceptance: Tasks can be created, moved left/right between columns and deleted
Each column shows its own count and is sorted by priority (high first)
Store methods are the only way state changes; all updates immutable
Board survives reload
task-card is presentational (inputs/outputs only)

hints: Per-column computed: readonly byStatus = computed(() => ({ todo: this.sorted().filter(t => t.status === 'todo'), ... })).
Moving: const order = ['todo', 'doing', 'done'] as const; find the index and add ±1, clamped to 0..2.
Priority sort: const rank = { high: 0, medium: 1, low: 2 }; [...tasks].sort((a, b) => rank[a.priority] - rank[b.priority]).

explainBack.q: Explain how a task moves from 'todo' to 'doing' through your components and store.
lookFor: column/board passes it to the store method

explainBack.q: Why is a priority rank map better than comparing strings?

lastHintExplanation: The card only emits 'move right' with its id; the store finds the task, replaces it with a copy whose status is the next column, and sets a new array. Computed per-column lists recalculate and Angular updates just those columns. Sorting with a rank map makes the intended order explicit; alphabetically, 'high' < 'low' < 'medium', which is wrong.

dsa.note: Keep a second stack (or pairs) so getMin is O(1).

title: Reusable UI components and content projection
goal: Build a small set of reusable UI components (button, card, modal, badge) with Tailwind and <ng-content>.

concepts: Content projection with <ng-content> and named slots (select="[slot=footer]")
Variant inputs: variant = input<'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger'>('primary')
Computing classes from inputs with computed()
host bindings for component root element classes
Accessible modal: role="dialog", aria-modal, Escape to close, focus on open
Keep UI components presentational and app-agnostic

Showcase page shows all variants
Task board refactored to use the UI components

hints:
Named slots: in ui-card's template and in use

Title

.
Classes: classes = computed(() => base + ' ' + variants[this.variant()] + ' ' + sizes[this.size()]); then [class]="classes()" on the inner <button>.

explainBack.q: Explain how content projection works in your ui-card.

title: Pipes and formatting
goal: Format dates, money and text in templates with built-in and custom pipes.

concepts: Built-in pipes: date, currency, number/decimal, percent, uppercase, titlecase, json, slice
Pipe parameters: {{ amount | currency:'INR':'symbol':'1.0-0' }}
Locale: registering en-IN for Indian number grouping
Writing a custom pure pipe with @Pipe and transform()
Pure pipes vs calling methods in templates (performance)
Chaining pipes

build.task: In angular-playground: format course prices with the currency pipe in INR with Indian grouping (register en-IN locale data and set LOCALE_ID), task dates with the date pipe ('d MMM y, h:mm a'), and progress with percent. Write 3 custom pure pipes with unit tests in their .spec.ts files: timeAgo (Date → '5 minutes ago'), initials ('Asha Rani' → 'AR'), and truncate (text, max = 40, with '…'). Use each somewhere in the app.
acceptance: Prices show like ₹1,49,999 (Indian grouping) using the currency pipe
Dates and percentages formatted with built-in pipes
3 custom pure pipes, each used in a template
Each custom pipe has at least 3 passing tests (ng test)
No method calls in templates that just format values

hints: Locale: in app.config.ts add registerLocaleData(localeEnIn) (import localeEnIn from '@angular/common/locales/en-IN') and provide { provide: LOCALE_ID, useValue: 'en-IN' }.
Pipe skeleton: @Pipe({ name: 'initials' }) export class InitialsPipe implements PipeTransform { transform(v: string): string { ... } } and add it to the component's imports.
Pipe test: const pipe = new InitialsPipe(); expect(pipe.transform('Asha Rani')).toBe('AR'); Run ng test.
proof: Commit with pipes and passing tests (paste the ng test summary in the commit message).

explainBack.q: Why is a pure pipe better than calling formatPrice(price) in a template?
lookFor: pure pipe re-runs only when its input changes
method calls run on every change detection

explainBack.q: How did you get Indian number grouping?

lastHintExplanation: A pure pipe is re-run only when its input value changes, while a method call in a template runs on every change detection pass. Pipes are also reusable and easy to unit test. Number formats depend on locale data, so registering en-IN and setting LOCALE_ID makes the currency pipe group digits as 1,49,999.

title: Debug lab: broken parent-child communication, and week review
goal: Fix input/output and binding mistakes between parent and child components.

concepts: value="x" passes a string; [value]="x" passes an expression
Output names must match the parent's (event) binding
Inputs are read-only signals in the child
Reading inputs too early (field initialisers) vs computed
Strict template type checking errors and how to read them

build.task: Add the two starter files to angular-playground (src/app/debug-rating/) and show <app-rating-demo /> on a page. Expected: 10 stars, the first 3 highlighted; clicking star 7 highlights 7 and the text says 'You rated 7 / 10'. There are 5 bugs across both files; some show up as compile errors. Fix each in its own commit. Write docs/week12-notes.md (Days 67–71: one confident and one weak topic each).

starterFiles.name: src/app/debug-rating/star-rating.ts
src/app/debug-rating/rating-demo.ts

acceptance: 10 stars render (max input respected)
Initial highlight shows 3 stars; clicking updates both stars and text
Child never assigns to its input; it emits an output
Parent binds with [value] and listens to the correct output name
5 fix commits; week12-notes.md written

hints: Start with the compile errors in the terminal. Assigning to this.value and comparing star <= value are both type errors: value is a signal, so read it with value().
Only 5 stars appear: stars is calculated once, when the class is created, before the parent's [max] arrives. Make it computed(() => ...) and use stars() in the template.
In the parent, value="rating()" without brackets is the literal string 'rating()'. The output is called changed, so (change) listens to the wrong event.
proof: Link to your final fix commit.

lookFor: stars from max() at field init → computed

explainBack.q: Why can't a child component set its own input?
lookFor: inputs are owned by the parent
child emits an event, parent updates state

lastHintExplanation: 1) stars is built once in a field initialiser, before the parent sets max; use computed(() => ...). 2) In the template, value is a signal and must be read as value(). 3) A child can't assign to its input; emit changed.emit(star) instead. 4) value="rating()" passes the literal text; use [value]="rating()". 5) The output is named changed, so the parent must listen with (changed).
